newsitem.title: USA: GM, union move closer to truck strike settlement.
newsitem.headline: GM, union move closer to truck strike settlement.

text.p: Bargainers moved closer to resolving a nine-week-old strike at General Motors Corp.'s truck plant here Wednesday as marathon talks continued, union officials said.
"They're getting close," said Larry Trandell, vice president of United Auto Workers Local 594. "Our bargaining chairman said it can be settled today, but they've still got a ways to go."
Negotiators for Local 594 and GM's Truck Group have been bargaining largely around the clock since about 8 a.m. Monday in an effort to resolve the strike, which began April 22.

About 5,800 people walked off the job at GM's Pontiac East full-size pickup truck assembly plant and related truck development and supply facilities on April 22 over demands for more jobs to ease an increasing workload.
Trandell said the manpower issue "is still on the table," but many other major grievances have been settled.

Other union officials said GM and the UAW have agreed on staffing levels at the truck assembly plant, but were still split over the union's demand for more new skilled trade apprentices in the Pontiac truck development operations.

Local 594 represents workers who build prototypes and test manufacturing processes at GM's new Truck Product Centre in Pontiac, which is responsible for designing and developing future truck models. Analysts say the strike has forced GM to slightly delay the introduction of its next-generation, 1999-model full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks.
But both GM and the UAW are motivated to resolve the strike prior to the automaker's annual summer shutdown, which runs from June 30 to July 14.

If the strike continues through the shutdown, strikers stand to lose an average of $850 in holiday pay, which many would welcome after subsisting more than two months on union strike benefits of only $150 a week.

GM would like to end the strike so it can begin retooling work during the shudown for the production of 1998 truck models. Union officials said the company needs a day of production to clear the assembly line of any partially completed trucks, which needs to occur by Saturday at the latest.
GM spokesman Dan Flores declined to characterise the progress of the talks, but said bargainers are taking only short breaks for food or naps.
"We're pleased that negotiations are intensifying and picking up," he said.
Separately, workers at the automaker's catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis., on Tuesday ratified a new local pact that averted a threatened strike at the facility by a 73 percent margin.

The agreement guarantees the plant will continue to build GM's catalytic converters through 2002 and prohibits GM from taking steps to shift any work at the plant to outside suppliers through 1998. The 870 workers at the plant also will receive at least $1,000 each to settle subcontracting grievances.

In addition, workers at GM's Grand Rapids, Mich., metal stamping plant are scheduled to vote Thursday on a new local contract reached there last week. Members of UAW Local 730 have rejected two previous tentative agreements.
